title: A 1965 Marketing Gimmick Invented The Health Goal You're Still Chasing
description:
The 10,000-step daily goal everyone quotes wasn't based on any health research at all. Here's where the number actually came from, and what real research says instead.

#shorts #wellbeing #sleepfacts #didyouknow

scenes.text: The goal of ten thousand steps a day isn't based on any health research at all. It came from a marketing campaign.
In 1965, a Japanese company called Yamasa released a pedometer named Manpo-kei, which literally translates to '10,000-steps meter.'
The number wasn't chosen from any study. Researchers say it was picked simply because it sounded good and was easy to remember, right as Tokyo's 1964 Olympics put fitness on the national radar.

One major study, tracking nearly seventeen thousand older women, found the real health benefit largely leveled off around seventy five hundred steps a day. Walking more didn't keep lowering their risk of death much further.
So the actual finding isn't 'walk less' -- it's that a marketing slogan from a 1960s Japanese gadget became a health rule nobody had actually tested.
Do you track your steps, and have you ever actually hit ten thousand in a day?
